Introduction
The investigation of time-dependent nuclear decay rates traces back to the origins of radioac-
tivity research. Notably, Maria Sk lodowska-Curie’s Ph.D. thesis [1] described an experiment
conducted to compare the radioactivity of uranium measured at midday and midnight, where
no significant variation was observed. In recent years, some studies have reported small periodic
modulations in the decay rates of various nuclei at the per mille level, with timescales ranging
from days to months and even up to a year (see [2] and references therein). However, other
researchers have challenged these findings, providing no evidence for such effects [3–5].
To shed light on this debated phenomenon, a set of precise γ-spectroscopy experiments were
conducted at the underground Gran Sasso Laboratory [6–9]. The unique advantages of this
facility, such as the rock overburden that significantly reduces the cosmic muon and neutron
fluxes, allowed the authors of Refs. [6–9] to minimize external influences.
This suppression
effectively eliminates the contribution of cosmic ray flux variations, which typically exhibit
annual modulations with amplitudes of a few percent [7]. Those measurements ultimately ruled
out modulations of the decay constants in several radioisotopes, such as 137Cs [6], 222Rn [7],
232Th [8], 40K and 226Ra [9], with amplitudes exceeding a few parts per 105 for periods between
a few hours and a year.
The aforementioned limits on the time modulation of radioisotope decay rates can also
be employed to derive stringent constraints on the time variation of fundamental constants
of nature, potentially arising from underlying fundamental physics. A particularly motivated
framework is that of the Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) axion [10–13], which simultaneously
addresses both the strong CP problem and the dark matter puzzle [14–16]. For a review of
recent experimental strategies for axion detection, see e.g. [17–19]. In particular, promoting
the QCD θ-term to a time-varying axion field enables a model-independent test of the axion-
gluon coupling through the oscillating electric dipole moment (EDM) of the neutron, induced
by the axion dark matter background [20–22]. Other approaches to set laboratory limits on the
axion-gluon coupling have been discussed e.g. in Refs. [23–29].
Recently, the authors of Ref. [30] have proposed to look for the time variation of the decay
rate of certain radioisotopes, focussing on the θ-dependence of β decay, previously developed
in [31]. This allowed them to set bounds on the axion coupling to gluons from tritium decay,
based on data taken at the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre [4].

Underground weak nuclear decay experiments
In the last 15 years several γ-spectroscopy experiments have been made in the underground
Gran Sasso Laboratory (LNGS) to search for a possible time dependence of the decay constant
of a few nuclei. In this section, we briefly describe two of those experiments, based on 40K [9]
and 137Cs [6], we discuss the obtained results in the framework of axion dark matter searches,
and finally present a new experimental setup currently under development.
We recall here the main advantage of the underground environment, which is to suppress
the varying background due to cosmic rays.
Specifically, the muon and neutron fluxes are
respectively suppressed by six and three orders of magnitude, compared to their levels at the
Earth’s surface, significantly reducing background noise and enhancing the precision of sensitive
measurements.
5.1
The 40K experiment
The 40K experiment started in September 2015 and ended in November 2017 [9]. A 4 liters
4”×4”×16” NaI crystal detects the 1461 keV γ-ray due to the electron capture decay of 40K
to the excited state of 40Ar. The source was made by about 9.6 kg of potassium bicarbonate
powder (KHCO3, corresponding to 3.8 kg of natural potassium, 0.0117% of which is 40K),
melted with 2.4 kg of paraffine grains contained inside a stainless steel box placed around the
NaI detector [9], whose light is detected by a photomultiplier. Finally, the signals from the
photomultiplier were processed by an Ortec digiBASE, a 14-pin photomultiplier base connected
to the photomultiplier itself. The whole setup was then shielded by at least 10 cm of lead and
housed in a dedicated container placed in front of Hall B of the LNGS.

Conclusions
In this work, we have investigated the time modulation of weak nuclear decays as a novel
method to explore axion dark matter. By developing a theoretical framework to compute the
θ-dependence of weak nuclear decays, including electron capture and β decay, we have predicted
the time variation of weak radioactivity induced by an oscillating axion dark matter background.
Recasting existing datasets on the weak nuclear decays of 40K [9] and 137Cs [6], collected at the
Gran Sasso Laboratory, allowed us to set constraints on the axion decay constant in the mass
range of few 10−23 eV to 10−19 eV. Furthermore, we proposed a new measurement based on
40K electron capture, enabling the exploration of shorter oscillation periods and axion masses
up to 10−9 eV.

In this work, we have investigated the time modulation of weak nuclear decays as a novel
method to explore axion dark matter. By developing a theoretical framework to compute the
θ-dependence of weak nuclear decays, including electron capture and β decay, we have predicted
the time variation of weak radioactivity induced by an oscillating axion dark matter background.
Recasting existing datasets on the weak nuclear decays of 40K [9] and 137Cs [6], collected at the
Gran Sasso Laboratory, allowed us to set constraints on the axion decay constant in the mass
range of few 10−23 eV to 10−19 eV. Furthermore, we proposed a new measurement based on
40K electron capture, enabling the exploration of shorter oscillation periods and axion masses
up to 10−9 eV.
